body: Thursday, March 06 2025 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto
Information available before 2025-03-06 00:00 UTC. Prices use completed prior sessions. Prepared retrospectively; later outcomes are excluded.

Macro Stance: Growth is slowing without breaking, and the Fed has no reason to move while the data stay mixed. Reuters reported that parts of the Treasury market are already worried about a pause in rate cuts [1]. February’s ISM services reading came in at 53.5 [2] and manufacturing at 50.3 [3], so activity is positive but thin. Private payrolls slowed: ADP showed US firms added 77,000 jobs, the smallest gain since July [4]. Weekly jobless claims jumped to 242,000 [5]. The Atlanta Fed model pointed to first-quarter growth of negative 1.5 percent [6], and WSJ framed the risk as stagflation [7].

Rates & Curve: The two-year yield is 3.99% and the 10-year is 4.28% at the prior close, with the 30-year at 4.57% (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05). The 10-year minus two-year spread is +29 bps, positively sloped and not steep. Over 20 observations the two-year fell 22 bps and the 10-year fell 24 bps, so the spread narrowed 2 bps: a bull flattening, with both yields lower and the 10-year lower by more. Over five observations the two-year is down 6 bps while the 10-year rose 3 bps, which says the rally has paused rather than reversed (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05). Equities show the strain. The S&P 500 closed at 5,842.63, up 1.12% in the prior session but down 3.23% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The VIX closed at 21.93 after a 27.43% rise over 20 sessions, and the dollar index stands at 105.74 index points, down 2.06% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

New / Most Important: The tariff sequence is the new fact. Trump’s Canada and Mexico duties were set to start on Tuesday, and stocks fell on the news [8]. Then the White House exempted some automakers for one month [9]. Reuters suggested pickup trucks explained the delay [10], carmakers were given a monthlong reprieve [11], and the New York Times noted that other levies continue [12]. The S&P 500 rose 1.12% in the prior session on that relief (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Relief is not removal: Automotive News warned that tariffs could wipe out Detroit 3 profits [13].

Playbook ✓: Hold the curve trade. The long end is rallying harder than the front, so stay long duration in the belly and avoid adding steepeners. Hold equities at market weight and buy protection through the tariff window while the VIX sits near 22, because a one-day rally does not remove the policy risk. Trim the consumer-discretionary names that have not shown they can pass tariffs on to customers. Change the call if the two-year yield climbs back above its 20-session reference of 4.21%, because that would mean the market is pricing the pause out of the curve (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05).

Macro Stance: Europe’s policy direction has changed. The ECB faces tougher calls ahead [14], but the bigger shift is fiscal. Germany’s parties agreed a historic overhaul of the debt brake to revamp the military and the economy [15]. Fortune put the package at $1.3 trillion [16], and the European Commission unveiled a €800bn plan to rearm Europe [17]. Markets are reading it as a regime change rather than a one-off.

Credit & Inflation: Credit is calmer than the currency suggests. Italy’s spread over Germany has dropped below 100 basis points [18], so the periphery risk premium that dominated the last crisis is now a footnote. Euro-area unemployment is 6.2 percent [19], with Italy improving but still among the highest. Inflation eased slightly in February [20], which gives the ECB room to stay patient. The DAX closed at 23,081.03, up 6.93% over 20 sessions, and the Euro Stoxx 50 at 5,489.12, up 4.14% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). EUR/USD is at 1.0627, up 2.45% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

New / Most Important: The DAX cleared 23,000 for the first time [21], and Reuters reported that stocks and the euro cheered the debt-brake deal while bonds fell [22]. The execution risk is real: Merz is still racing to win support for the package [23], and Bloomberg wrote that Germany is loosening its fiscal chains to transform European defence [24]. The cleanest expression is in defence and the industrials that supply it, and European defence shares have hit record highs [25].

Playbook ✓: Stay overweight European cyclicals and domestic-facing banks against the US multiple, and keep a defence-supplier position sized to the spending rather than to the news flow. Add on pullbacks that hold the DAX above its 20-session reference of 21,585.93 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-05). What would change the call is a failed parliamentary vote on the package, which would take the German leadership out of the trade.

Macro Stance: Beijing’s 2025 framework is expansionary on paper. The government set growth at around 5% [26] and an inflation goal of around 2% [27], and it set the deficit at around 4% of GDP, a record [28]. Bloomberg put the official budget deficit at its highest in more than 30 years [29]. Reuters described the stimulus as a response to changes unseen in a century [30], and it reported that Beijing put consumer spending ahead of technology [31]. The message is that Beijing will spend to protect growth against tariffs rather than wait for them to fade.

PMIs & Activity: The surveys show a rebound from a soft base. Reuters reported that factory activity picked up in February, though trade uncertainty weighed on the outlook [32]. The non-manufacturing index was 50.4 in February [33], which keeps services barely in expansion. January’s private factory survey had shown growth slowing [34], so the February pickup is a recovery from a low rather than a new cycle. Prices are still soft: consumer inflation was 0.5% in January [35], and producer deflation persisted [36]. In Hong Kong, retail sales value fell 3.2% in January [37], a reminder that the consumer is still soft even as stocks rally.

Credit Impulse: Credit turned up at the start of the year. Reuters reported that China’s January bank lending hit a record high on policy stimulus [38], and that the property loan contraction eased after government support [39]. The fiscal window widened as Beijing stepped up spending to counter the tariffs [40]. The impulse is front-loaded, so the test is whether lending holds its pace once the January surge fades.

Property: Property is still the drag. A Reuters poll sees home prices falling further, with no recovery until 2026 [41]. Second-hand home prices narrowed their decline for a seventh straight month in February, a report said [42]. The Financial Times wrote that the state is propping up the housing market [43], and Reuters reported that hedge funds are betting on a turnaround in the unloved sector [44]. The Economist framed the policy moment as a test of Xi Jinping on deflation [45]. Improvement in the monthly data is still only a narrowing of the decline. Hong Kong’s banks face rising risks amid the prolonged property slump, Moody’s warned [46].

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Trade is the policy story. China hit back at US farm goods with extra tariffs of 10% to 15% [47], and its extra duties of up to 15% on some US goods start on March 10 [48]. It added 15 US companies to its export control list [49] and banned imports of Illumina’s gene sequencers [50]. Beijing is still signalling a willingness to talk while it retaliates [51]. Defence spending rises 7.2% in 2025 [52], and Beijing plans to boost food imports from Latin America and Europe as the trade war escalates [53]. Fiscal support is the offset.

Markets & Flows: Equities carry the rally. The Hang Seng closed at 23,594.21, up 2.84% in the prior session and 14.55% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The Shanghai Composite closed at 3,341.97 index points, up 3.48% over 20 sessions. The China A-share ETF ASHR closed at 27.02 USD, and KWEB, the China internet ETF, closed at 36.68 USD, up 14.95% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). USD/CNY closed at 7.2651, up 1.16% over 20 sessions, so the currency is steady (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). S&P Global wrote that Chinese equities are on track for a major boost from an insurance investment directive [54], and TradingView reported Asian markets rallying as Alibaba jumped on its AI push [55]. Hong Kong’s listing market is running hot as well: the bubble-tea chain Mixue popped 47% on debut as Hong Kong IPO volumes rebounded [56].

New / Most Important: The insurance directive is the most important signal, because it is a lever aimed at the equity market itself rather than at the growth targets [54]. Reuters reported that Trump’s cheap-yuan comment is unfounded, which removes one of the currency arguments against Chinese assets [57]. The fiscal tilt is visible in the numbers: the official budget deficit is at its highest in more than 30 years [29]. The Hang Seng’s 2.84% gain in the prior session shows the market is already acting on it (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Playbook ✓: Own the internet and platform names on dips, using KWEB as the liquid vehicle, and keep USD/CNY exposure small because the currency is steady at 7.2651. Add on a Shanghai Composite close that holds above its 20-session reference of 3,229.49 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-05). Cut if the insurance directive is not followed by inflows. ⚠ Divergence: the Hang Seng is up 14.55% over 20 sessions while the property data still show home prices falling, so equities are running ahead of the real-economy evidence (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Macro Stance: Japan is leaving easy policy, and the bond market is running ahead of the central bank. The 10-year yield hit its highest level in over 15 years [58], and CNBC put it near 16-year highs on rate-hike expectations and a global sell-off [59]. Inflation keeps the BOJ on its hike path [60]: the inflation rate climbed to a 2-year high of 4% in January [61]. The BOJ governor warned of strong global uncertainty from US tariffs [62], which is the counterweight to the hike case.

Activity & Currency: Traders have placed a record bet on a stronger yen, eyeing further rate hikes [63]. USD/JPY closed at 149.7990, down 2.81% over 20 sessions from 154.1330 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The Nikkei 225 closed at 37,418.24, down 2.86% over 20 sessions, though it rose 0.23% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Corporate spending is pulling back: Reuters reported that Japanese capex dropped for the first time in four years amid tariff fears [64], and Sony and Suntory are building US stockpiles as the tariff threat grows [65]. Yen-selling pressure persists despite Trump’s warning shot, Nikkei Asia reported [66].

Playbook ✓: Trim the Nikkei into strength and hedge yen exposure for dollar-based holders, since a stronger yen cuts the value of overseas earnings while the front end prices hikes. Favour domestic-rate beneficiaries only on a pullback. Change the call if USD/JPY breaks back above 150, which would mean the yen trade has run out of room and the tariff drag on exporters becomes the dominant risk (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Macro Stance: Australia’s activity data gave the RBA room to keep a hawkish tone. GDP grew 1.3% in the fourth quarter, supported by exports [67], and Bloomberg tied the print to the central bank’s hawkish tone [68]. The growth rate hit a two-year high [69], and the economy exited a 21-month per-capita recession [70]. The AFR published the chart the RBA used to justify its latest rate cut [71], which is the anchor for the next decision.

Demand & Financing: Households are the swing factor. CoreLogic data show the housing market ending its downturn as the rate cut lifted sentiment [72]. Chalmers is upbeat, but economists warn of a shallow recovery [73]. The bank trade is the nervous point: short sellers ditched CBA as sell-off doubts mounted [74], and CBA completed its exit from Vietnam’s VIB after a 4.4% stake sale [75]. The ASX 200 closed at 8,141.10, down 3.28% over 20 sessions from 8,416.90 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). AUD/USD closed at 0.6270, up 0.30% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), and Fortescue, the iron ore miner, closed at 15.93 AUD, down 16.11% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Playbook ✓: Own the growth beneficiaries rather than the banks until short interest in CBA falls, and keep AUD exposure small against a dollar that is still drifting lower. Miners with iron ore exposure need the commodity to steady before they re-rate. What would change the call: a sharper fall in the AUD or a clear reversal in bank short interest. ⚠ Divergence: the GDP print says growth is firm [68], but the ASX is down 3.28% over 20 sessions, so the equity market is discounting the bank and dividend story rather than the macro upturn (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Macro Stance: Poland’s cycle is turning up, and the central bank has to watch inflation. Manufacturing shows signs of recovery for the first time in almost three years [76], and a PMI reading signalled the end of an almost three-year industrial recession [77]. GDP grew 2.9% in 2024, beating forecasts [78], and the latest quarterly reading showed acceleration, though below what was expected [79]. Inflation is still the constraint: Business Insider Polska called rising prices a strong argument for the central bank on rates [80], and January’s consumer prices edged higher [81]. Wages rose strongly in 2024, the statistics office showed [82], and the finance minister called 2025 a breakthrough year as the economy accelerates [83]. Poland and Czechia have the lowest unemployment in the European Union, according to Eurostat [84].

Markets: The zloty is the trade. Bloomberg reported the zloty at a 10-year high against the dollar, fanned by a hawkish central bank [85], and Rzeczpospolita reported it beating a seven-year record [86]. USD/PLN closed at 3.9165, down 3.45% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), and EUR/PLN at 4.1608, down 1.11% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Parkiet asked whether a strong zloty will carry the WIG20 to a new record [87]. The WIG20 total-return tracker closed at 49.23 PLN, up 8.07% over 20 sessions, and the US-listed Poland ETF EPOL closed at 26.92 USD, up 14.12% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Foreigners are in the bond market: more than ten central banks hold Polish treasuries [88], and Money.pl reported foreign central banks buying them [89]. Parkiet’s fear index is the sentiment check [90].

Fiscal & Politics: Fiscal policy is the weak point. Economist Leszek Balcerowicz criticised the Tusk government for spending that makes no sense [91], and Bankier.pl quoted him again on spending that serves no purpose [92]. The finance minister’s line is that 2025 is a breakthrough year [83], which is the government’s answer. Whether credit holidays come back is in doubt, and the government is pointing to another solution [93]. Politics is a risk: a far-right candidate’s rise has turned the presidential race into a three-horse contest [94], and Politico wrote that Poland’s nationalists stick to Trump like glue [95].

Corporate & Sectors: Earnings separate the quality names. Orlen posted a record profit [96] and a historic dividend [97], and its Czech refineries are again without Russian oil but have a Western alternative [98]. PKN closed at 63.27 PLN, up 15.35% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Bank Pekao made 6.4 billion zloty and wants half of it for dividends [99]; PEO closed at 170.20 PLN, up 9.10% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Dino Polska hit a record high on a weak market [100] and presented its 2025 plans [101]; DNP closed at 488.20 PLN, up 6.90% over 20 sessions. At mBank, 25 thousand franc-loan borrowers have settled [102], and MBK closed at 736.00 PLN, up 20.03% over 20 sessions. Business Insider Polska reported a series of seismic shocks at two KGHM mines [103], and PGE is discussing a second nuclear plant at Bełchatów [104]. CD Projekt drew attention for its Witcher 4 character design, with the studio explaining the changes [105], but it is a product story rather than an earnings one.

Geopolitics & Security: Defence is the demand driver. Poland said it will spend 4.7% of GDP on defence this year [106], and Poland and South Korea signed a security agreement [107]. Poland sent a large batch of T-72 tanks to Ukraine [108], and it revealed what the Starlink terminals for Ukraine cost [109]. Russian operatives were reportedly paid to paint anti-government graffiti in Poland [110], and the Polish space agency is investigating a cyberattack on its systems [111]. Defence producers are the market’s clearest winners in Warsaw [112]. Ukrainian stocks surged on the Warsaw exchange in February on talk of a peace plan [113].

New / Most Important: The one signal that matters is the PMI turn, because it moves the story from currency carry to real growth. Manufacturing is recovering for the first time in almost three years [76], which is why the zloty and the WIG20 can rise together. Santander Bank warned that a strong zloty may weigh on GDP [114]: the same currency strength that draws foreign money also cuts into the export earnings that carry the recovery.

Playbook ✓: Buy the banks and the defence names on pullbacks, keep zloty exposure, and hedge only on a 20-session move against you. Change the call if the next inflation print surprises higher, because that would push back the date at which rates can fall. ⚠ Divergence: the zloty and the WIG20 are rising on growth hopes while the fiscal criticism is getting louder [91], so the market is pricing the growth recovery but not the budget.

Narrative: Technology is carrying the consensus and losing the tape. The technology sector ETF closed at 221.57 USD, up 1.41% in the prior session but down 4.07% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The AI case is intact at the software layer: Microsoft’s $13 billion OpenAI investment cleared a UK review [115], and Apple’s App Store revenue rose 14% as ChatGPT drove growth [116].

Reported: Apple cut the price of its MacBook Air by $100 despite tariffs [117], and Intel defeated a shareholder lawsuit over foundry losses that the headline puts at $32 billion [118]. Dell’s full-year 2025 earnings per share beat expectations [119].

EPS Upside Watch: Dell is set up for upside on capital returns. It raised its dividend 18% and launched a $10 billion buyback [120] after its earnings beat, and the buyback is the part of the story the market can count.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says AI demand cannot be stopped. The counter-signal is that Nvidia’s optimistic forecast failed to convince Wall Street [121], and that a Summit Insights downgrade cited AI market concerns [122]. Nvidia shares fell 9% on tariff fears [123].

Narrative: Communication services has lost momentum even though the AI advertising story is intact. The sector ETF closed at 101.47 USD, down 1.98% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), and Alphabet is the drag, down 16.16% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Google announced layoffs in its HR and cloud units as part of ongoing cost cuts [124], and an advertising outage cost tens of thousands in ad revenue over a weekend [125].
Reported: Warner Bros. Discovery added 6.4 million Max subscribers and forecast 150 million by the end of 2026 [126]. That is the growth case in the sector.

EPS Upside Watch: Disney is set up for margin upside rather than revenue upside. It cut 6% of its ABC network and entertainment TV workforce [127] and shut the data-driven website 538 [128]. That cost discipline shows up first in margins.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The AI-winner reading meets cost cuts. An upgrade said Alphabet’s future looks brighter than the Big Tech alternatives, pointing to Waymo and Willow [129], while the same company is cutting staff in its cloud and HR units [124]. The consensus cannot hold both, so the stock is being read as an option on AI rather than as a cost story.

Narrative: Banks have the cleanest earnings story and the most fragile credit story. The financial sector ETF closed at 50.21 USD, up 0.58% in the prior session and down 1.82% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). JPMorgan closed at 251.53 USD, down 6.12% over 20 sessions, and Goldman Sachs at 593.07 USD, down 6.48%, while the regional bank ETF KRE is down 8.34% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Reported: Goldman Sachs’ full-year 2024 results beat expectations [130], and BNY Mellon’s revenue beat while earnings per share were in line [131]. Customers Bancorp missed on EPS [132], and Ready Capital’s shares plunged 28% after a fourth-quarter loss and a dividend cut [133].

EPS Upside Watch: Investment banks and asset managers are set up for upside if deal flow holds. Blackstone beat its full-year expectations [134], and Millennium committed $1 billion to a stock picker [135]. Banks are regaining ground in lending as private credit eases off mega loan deals [136].

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consumer-credit story is the counter-signal. Fitch says credit card performance is deteriorating [137], and credit spreads are on their longest widening streak since 2023 [138]. Earnings can beat while the loan book weakens.

Narrative: Energy has lost its geopolitical premium as supply keeps coming. WTI closed at 66.31 USD, down 8.79% over 20 sessions, and Brent at 69.30 USD, down 9.06% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The energy ETF closed at 85.70 USD, down 4.82% over 20 sessions. OPEC+ agreed to gradually hike output from April [139], and February output rose as Iran’s exports kept flowing [140].

Reported: Saudi Aramco posted a drop in full-year profit and slashed its dividend [141], and it expects a lower 2025 dividend after net income fell [142]. Colombia’s Ecopetrol saw profit slide 22% in 2024 [143].

EPS Upside Watch: Natural gas is the only energy line with upside in the price data. Henry Hub natural gas closed at 4.45 USD per MMBtu, up 36.80% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Oil names have no upside surprise on current prices.
⚡ Breaking Convention: The geopolitical premium that supports oil is failing to hold, and one commentary argued that Trump has exposed OPEC’s diminished market power [144].

Narrative: Defence and aerospace lead the sector’s story, and Europe’s rearmament is the engine. The industrial sector ETF closed at 133.85 USD, down 2.31% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Europe announced an $840 billion rearmament plan that sent BAE and Thales soaring [145], and Citi said Lockheed and five other defence stocks look like buys after a slump [146].
Reported: Thales’ shares soared after its 2024 results beat forecasts on defence spending [147]. Bunzl’s shares fell on lower pretax profit [148].

EPS Upside Watch: Boeing is set up for upside only on execution. Its CEO told staff the company must change its insular culture [149], and a joint venture was selected to build the South Carolina site expansion [150]. Boeing closed at 163.16 USD, down 7.42% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Defence demand is not the constraint in this sector; execution is. Emirates said it will spend $5 billion refitting its aircraft [151], and Boeing’s culture problem [149] is the reason to doubt that aircraft supply can keep up with demand.

Narrative: The consumer sector is absorbing the tariff shock, and the names with pricing power are telling the story. The consumer discretionary ETF closed at 211.41 USD, down 8.80% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Best Buy warned that price increases from tariffs were “highly likely” [152].

Reported: Target’s sales fell but its earnings topped expectations [153]. Adidas’ fourth-quarter sales topped expectations as its final Yeezy stock sold off [154], and Foot Locker’s results show the sneaker industry, and Nike, still have more pain ahead [155].

EPS Upside Watch: Target is set up for a surprise only if its growth plan works. It unveiled a $15 billion sales growth strategy [156] while bracing for first-quarter profit pressure from tariffs and low demand [157].

⚡ Breaking Convention: Tesla is the consumer-discretionary story in one stock. Its China-made EV sales fell to their lowest since August 2022 [158], and the shares are down 28.84% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The sector reads as weak across the board, but brand-led names are being judged on their own stories.

Narrative: Staples are the defensive trade, and the defence is working for some names. The staples ETF closed at 82.44 USD, up 4.86% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Coca-Cola closed at 70.08 USD, up 11.82% over 20 sessions, and PepsiCo at 153.88 USD, up 7.24% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
Reported: Unilever and Procter & Gamble profits came under pressure as shoppers turned to smaller food brands [159]. Target’s chief said Mexico’s tariffs could raise produce prices within days [160].

EPS Upside Watch: Walmart and Costco are set up on trade-down. Shoppers moving to cheaper formats favour the value channel [159], and Costco closed at 1,047.75 USD, up 2.53% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The upside sits with the stores that absorb the shift, not with the brands losing share.
⚡ Breaking Convention: Japanese consumers are hunting for bargains as food inflation bites [161], which cuts against the pricing-power story that supports staples multiples.

Narrative: Obesity drugs are the sector’s growth story and its price problem. Eli Lilly closed at 929.72 USD, up 12.55% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Novo Nordisk is selling Wegovy for $499 a month to cash-paying US customers [162], after cutting its prices in a move that followed Eli Lilly’s [163]. Amgen started two late-stage trials for its MariTide obesity drug [164].
Reported: UnitedHealth’s full-year 2024 earnings missed expectations [165], and AstraZeneca’s shares rose 3% after a regulatory approval that expands the use of its cancer drug Imfinzi [166].

EPS Upside Watch: Eli Lilly is set up for upside on estimate revisions. Wells Fargo kept its Buy rating and raised its target to $1,100 [167]. The price cut is the risk to watch, not a reason to be short.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus treats pricing power as safe, and Novo’s cash price cut says otherwise [162]. Lilly’s gain comes while its rival is cutting price [163], so the sector’s margin story now depends on volume.

Narrative: Materials are a tariff trade, not a growth trade. Copper closed at 4.77 USD, up 9.76% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Bloomberg reported that US copper prices surged as Trump signalled a 25% tariff on imports [168]. Copper is an asset priced for the grid and data-centre build, and this rally is about the tariff and the supply, not about China’s growth.
Reported: Fortescue, the iron ore miner, is down 16.11% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), and iron ore volatility sparked global concern, OilPrice.com reported [169].

EPS Upside Watch: Gold miners are set up for upside if the dollar keeps losing ground. The dollar index is down 2.06% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), and a Reuters poll sees the dollar losing its lustre on trade war jitters [170]. Newmont closed at 43.85 USD, up 1.15% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The copper-as-growth-gauge reading does not fit this tape. The metal is rising on tariffs and supply, while China’s non-manufacturing index at 50.4 [33] is barely expanding. That makes copper an asset to own for its own reasons, not a signal about China.

Narrative: Real estate is getting the rate tailwind. The 10-year yield is down 24 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05), and the 30-year mortgage rate is the lowest since October [171]. The real estate ETF closed at 43.42 USD, up 5.01% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
Reported: Green Street reported a large-format retail asset sold on a 6.14% yield [172], and JLL said investment appetite for grocery-anchored retail remains robust [173].

EPS Upside Watch: Mortgage-linked names are set up for upside if rates keep easing. Homebuyers are making bigger down payments but still struggle to raise the cash [174], and a lower rate eases that constraint first.
⚡ Breaking Convention: The rate story has a cost story. Rising property insurance costs are stressing multifamily housing [175], and tariffs could raise new-home prices for buyers [176].

Narrative: The AI power trade is fading. Constellation closed at 229.32 USD, down 25.14% over 20 sessions, and Vistra at 126.87 USD, down 24.63% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). CNBC wrote that the power stock at the centre of the AI trade is fading as impatient investors await a data-centre deal [177]. The utilities ETF closed at 77.49 USD, down 0.15% over 20 sessions.
Reported: Sempra’s shares slumped after a dour 2025 profit forecast on high costs [178]. Edison International said the cause of the Eaton fire could take 12 to 18 months to determine [179].

EPS Upside Watch: Contracted renewables are the safer upside. Demand for renewable energy projects remains strong, but supply is growing [180], so contract wins matter more than power prices. US small modular reactor deals remain elusive for NuScale [181], which keeps that upside on the watch list.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Retail sentiment on Vistra turned bearish on the “mega growth” case after DeepSeek [182], which cuts against the AI-power consensus. The consensus expects data-centre demand to lift every power name, while the market is discounting the ones without a signed deal.

Narrative: European autos are absorbing three policy changes at once: US tariffs, the emissions debate and a push toward cheaper EVs. The iShares STOXX Europe 600 Automobiles & Parts ETF closed at 52.16 EUR, down 6.02% over five sessions and up 1.14% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Reuters reported that European auto stocks sank as US tariffs on Mexico and Canada kicked in [183].
Reported: Continental’s shares plunged on a revenue fall and soft guidance [184]. Mercedes is cutting headcount and lowering pay increases in its cost-cutting drive [185].

EPS Upside Watch: Volkswagen’s budget EV is the upside story. VW unveiled an entry-level EV aimed at squeezed European consumers [186], with a production version set to launch at around 20,000 euros [187]. Volkswagen closed at 105.55 EUR, up 13.03% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

⚡ Breaking Convention: The emissions rule is contested. One report says the Commission will water down auto emission targets [188], while another says the EU sticks to its zero-emission path for new cars [189]. The two readings do not settle the direction, so the sector’s multiple depends on which one the market believes.

Narrative: Semiconductors are caught between the AI cycle and the tariff map. The semiconductor ETF closed at 206.63 USD, down 5.19% over five sessions and 4.51% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). TSMC’s $100 billion US commitment is real, but it will not include the most advanced chips, Taiwan confirmed [190], and Qualcomm’s CEO welcomed the investment [191].
Reported: ASML’s annual report says export curbs hit customer spending in 2024 [192]. Nvidia and Broadcom are testing chips on Intel’s manufacturing process, sources said [193].

EPS Upside Watch: Nvidia’s China business is the upside watch, if the indirect channel holds. Tom’s Hardware reported that Chinese firms get Blackwell chips by ordering through nearby countries, defying US bans [194]. That is volume a tighter export rule would remove.

⚡ Breaking Convention: A Chinese scientist urged China to build an alternative to Nvidia’s CUDA software [195], which cuts against the software moat that supports the chip multiple. Investors cannot treat that moat as safe while an alternative is being pushed.

Rewarded: Forward numbers and cash returns were rewarded. Rolls-Royce upgraded its forecasts and its shares soared over 18% [196]. Synopsys’s revenue forecast beat estimates on the AI chip boom, and the shares rose [197]. Snowflake posted a big earnings beat and the stock jumped [198]. Thales soared as its 2024 earnings beat forecasts on defence spending [147]. Dell lifted its dividend 18% and launched a $10 billion buyback [120] after its full-year EPS beat [119].

Punished: Beats with soft forward numbers were punished. Nvidia’s sales grew 78% with strong guidance [199], yet Reuters reported its optimistic forecast did not convince Wall Street [121], and the stock sank over 8% as earnings were no match for sky-high expectations [200]. Salesforce missed on revenue and issued disappointing guidance [201]. Norwegian Cruise Line’s shares fell despite an earnings beat [202].

Pattern: The pattern is that the market pays for the next quarter, not the last one. Trailing beats were ignored when the forward number was soft, and the rewards went to companies that raised forward numbers or returned cash. The sharpest disappointment came where the beat was already in the price. Nvidia dropped in the session after its optimistic report [203].

Attention into EPS: Attention is moving to the next print. Stocktwits flagged Vistra’s retail sentiment as bearish before its results, in the “mega growth” debate after DeepSeek [182]. Nvidia was downgraded by Summit Insights over AI market concerns [122]. The template for the next cycle is consumer guidance on tariffs: Best Buy’s warning that price increases were “highly likely” [152] is what investors will check first.

Playbook: Own the names that raise forward numbers or return cash, and sell the beats that come with soft guidance. Hedge the AI leaders into the next print, because a priced-in beat can cost 8% in a day, as Nvidia’s drop showed [200]. Trade the consumer names on tariff guidance rather than on the revenue line.

Attention Gap: Reactor and uranium names have fallen while the coverage chases the AI trade that needs them. Oklo closed at 30.29 USD, down 35.40% over 20 sessions, NuScale at 17.32 USD, down 24.63%, and Cameco at 42.99 USD, down 14.57% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The news is about deals, not demand: Oklo closed its acquisition of a radioisotope producer [204], and Siemens Energy will supply Rolls-Royce with equipment for small reactors [205].

Exposure & Risk: The instruments are the uranium ETF URA, closed at 24.67 USD and down 14.67% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), and the single names OKLO and SMR. The risk is a deal drought: US small modular reactor deals remain elusive for NuScale [181], and the high-beta names move on news alone.

Trigger to Watch: A signed hyperscaler power contract, the event CNBC says the market is waiting for [177]. Italy’s plan to return to nuclear power [206] is a policy tailwind that will not move the stocks on its own.

Attention Gap: Regional banks are quiet compared with private credit, which the coverage treats as the growth story. The regional bank ETF closed at 58.71 USD, down 8.34% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). AFR asked how to access the private credit boom [207], while Fitch’s warning on card performance [137] is the counter-signal for the lenders.

Exposure & Risk: The instrument is the regional bank ETF KRE, down 4.02% over five sessions and 8.34% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The risk is a credit-cycle bet: Ready Capital’s shares plunged 28% after a fourth-quarter loss and a dividend cut [133], and cuts like that spread when the loan book weakens.
Trigger to Watch: A second regional lender missing on EPS after Customers Bancorp did [132]. If the misses cluster, the theme becomes consensus within one reporting season.

Attention Gap: Japanese corporate restructuring is covered as a deal story, not as a capital-return story. Seven & i said it is selling its supermarket operations and announcing a massive buyback [208], and KKR and Walmart agreed to sell the Seiyu supermarket chain for $2.5 billion [209]. Toyota closed at 2,849.50 JPY, up 4.57% over five sessions, and Sony at 3,583.00 JPY, up 6.01% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Exposure & Risk: The instruments are single names in Tokyo and the Japan ETF EWJ, which closed at 70.15 USD, up 2.75% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The risk is the currency: a stronger yen cuts the dollar value of yen buybacks for foreign holders, and USD/JPY sits at 149.7990 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
Trigger to Watch: The 10-year yield, which has reached its highest level in over 15 years [58]. A further rise would re-rate the financials and test the buyback case in yen.

Attention Gap: Emerging-market bonds get little airtime while the coverage is about tariffs. Morningstar asked whether emerging-market stocks could outperform US stocks [210], and The DESK reported that inflows to emerging-market debt beta funds could change trading patterns [211]. The dollar emerging-market bond ETF EMB closed at 91.28 USD, up 0.78% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Exposure & Risk: The instrument is EMB. The risk is a dollar rebound: the dollar index is at 105.74 index points and fell 2.06% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), so a reversal would hit the bonds.

Trigger to Watch: A further break below 105 in the dollar index, which CoinDesk reported had already happened as bitcoin surged [212]. A dollar that stays under that level keeps the carry trade intact.

Market Context: Bitcoin closed at 90,623.56 USD, up 3.90% in the latest session and 7.41% over five sessions, but down 6.21% over 20 sessions from 96,623.87 on February 13 (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-05). Ether closed at 2,241.98 USD, down 16.22% over 20 sessions; Solana at 146.27 USD, down 24.78%; and XRP at 2.50 USD, up 16.54% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-05). The bitcoin ETF IBIT closed at 51.44 USD, down 8.36% over 20 sessions, and Coinbase at 222.45 USD, down 20.66% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Strategy closed at 308.55 USD, up 17.20% over five sessions and down 11.42% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Bitcoin plunged $10,000 in a day as crypto leaders criticised the plan [213], then popped 6% on a hint that the reserve strategy was near [214].

New / Most Important: The reserve is still a promise without a date. The White House hosts its first crypto summit on Friday [215], and a trader eyeing a retest of $78K said the US is seen delaying the reserve [216]. Open interest in bitcoin hit its lowest level since August [217], so leverage is light and a clear reserve size would move the market quickly. Flows are the risk: the crypto market saw a record $2.9 billion of outflows [218], and spot bitcoin ETFs once bled more than $1 billion in one day [219] before an eight-day outflow streak ended [220]. El Salvador says it will keep buying bitcoin despite IMF pressure [221].

Playbook: Hold bitcoin in spot-type vehicles, size for a retest of $78K, and add only when ETF inflows return and open interest rebuilds. Treat Strategy as a levered proxy: its 20-session decline of 11.42% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05) is what leverage looks like on the way down. Trim into the reserve pops. The 96,623.87 February reference is the line: above it the reserve premium is back, below it the trade is a fade.

Global Liquidity: Liquidity is still abundant even as policy tightens at the margin. The New York Fed’s Perli said market liquidity levels remain abundant [222]. India’s central bank announced an infusion of over $21 billion to support growth [223] and signalled it wants a banking-system liquidity surplus [224]. The Boston Fed’s work on dealer risk constraints shows that relaxing them can make the Treasury market more liquid [225], which matters because a crowded trade depends on that plumbing. The euro area is on the same plumbing, with the ECB publishing its January bank rate statistics [226].

Rates & Dollar: The dollar is the swing factor. The dollar index is at 105.74 index points, down 2.06% over 20 sessions and down 0.64% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). CoinDesk reported the index declining below 105 as bitcoin surged past $88,000 [212], and a Reuters poll says the dollar will lose its lustre on trade war jitters [170]. Long bonds are the other side of the trade: TLT closed at 90.70 USD, up 2.57% over 20 sessions, and IEF at 94.56 USD, up 1.66% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). On the curve, the two-year is down 22 bps and the 10-year down 24 bps over 20 observations, a bull flattening (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05). Reuters reported that parts of the Treasury market are concerned about a pause in rate cuts [1].

Credit Check: Credit is wider in the middle of the market. Bloomberg reported that credit spreads are on their longest widening streak since 2023 [138], and Fitch says credit card performance is deteriorating [137]. High yield has held: HYG closed at 79.62 USD, up 0.14% over 20 sessions and down 0.55% over five, while investment-grade LQD closed at 108.83 USD, up 1.28% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The junk market has not yet followed the widening. In Europe, Italy’s spread over Germany has dropped below 100 basis points [18], so the regional credit picture is not uniform.

Equity & Fund Flows: Buybacks are the main equity bid. Dell raised its dividend 18% and launched a $10 billion buyback [120], and Trip.com announced a US$400M buyback as its stock fell 12% [227]. AppLovin’s shares bounced back after its buyback news [228], and LSEG’s shares rose on a $633.8 million buyback [229]. Fund flows are mixed: spot bitcoin ETFs have seen record outflows [219], and inflows returned once an 8-day outflow streak ended [220]. The strategists are cautious. MarketWatch wrote that Wall Street’s biggest bear says the S&P 500 could drop to 4,200 [230], and Goldman Sachs warned the rally may falter after a 5% selloff [231]. The S&P 500 is down 3.23% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Hedge funds had a rough February as well, with the sector’s biggest names stung in the month [232].

Portfolio Implication: Keep equity at market weight, hedge tail risk, and prefer buyback-backed earnings over momentum with no cash behind it. Own duration: a bull flattening with the long end leading is money moving into the long end, and the 10-year is down 24 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05). Keep credit beta small until spreads stop widening. The conditional is the dollar: a break below 105 would help emerging-market hard-currency debt, where EMB closed at 91.28 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Cash is a position too: Berkshire Hathaway’s market value reached $1.07 trillion, surpassing Tesla [233], and Barron’s noted that Warren Buffett has been selling stocks [234].

What Is Priced: The market is pricing a soft payroll print. ADP showed US firms added 77,000 jobs, the smallest gain since July [4], and a Reuters week-ahead piece framed rising investor angst as about to be tested by the jobs data [235]. Gold’s pause has been explained as a wait for the same report [236]. The two-year yield is down 22 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05), so part of a weak print is already in the front end.

Conditional Expression: If the next jobs report confirms the ADP slowdown, the front end rallies and the flattening deepens, so buy duration on the weak print and avoid steepeners. If hiring holds, the two-year should retrace part of its 22 bps fall, and the dollar index at 105.74 index points would firm again (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Risk: The risk is a strong official number against weak private payrolls, which would leave the two-year at 3.99% and the S&P 500 at 5,842.63 exposed to a rate scare (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05).

What Is Priced: Trade policy now runs on dates. Carmakers got a monthlong reprieve from tariffs [11], and Trump exempted some automakers from the Canada and Mexico levies for one month [9]. China’s extra tariffs of up to 15% on some US goods start on March 10 [48], and Mexico said it would detail its retaliation on Sunday [237].

Conditional Expression: If the automaker pause is extended, the European and Japanese auto names keep their rebound and the S&P 500 keeps the 1.12% gain of the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). If it lapses, the autos are the first casualty. Watch the farm trade as well, since Reuters reported China targeting US soybeans and lumber in its response [238].

Risk: The risk is an escalation on the Mexican side that takes the one-month reprieve off the table. Automotive News said tariffs could wipe out Detroit 3 profits [13], which is the cost the reprieve only postpones.

What Is Priced: The market has priced the direction of Germany’s fiscal turn, not the arithmetic. Reuters reported the parties agreed a historic overhaul [15], and Merz is still racing to win support for the package [23]. The DAX closed at 23,081.03, up 6.93% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Conditional Expression: If the package passes, German and European defence, infrastructure and industrial names keep the leadership, and Rheinmetall, which closed at 1,202.50 EUR and is up 60.59% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05), keeps its bid. If support slips, the defence leaders are the most exposed. The Euro Stoxx 50, at 5,489.12, is the broad test.

Risk: The risk is that a stock up 60.59% in 20 sessions has priced the package before it is law. Bloomberg reported that East German voters complicate Merz’s plan to boost Ukraine defence [239], which is the political drag.

What Is Priced: Shutdown risk is back on the table. CNN reported that Democrats rejected the GOP funding strategy and stoked shutdown fears [240], and Politico wrote that Democrats are serious about a shutdown [241]. Axios reported that Republicans are hunting for Democratic votes to avoid one [242].

Conditional Expression: If Republicans find the votes, the shutdown premium fades and the safe-haven bid in gold and Treasuries comes off. If they do not, expect the bid to return, with gold at 2,926.00 USD as the cleanest hedge (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Risk: The risk is a political shock landing on a tape that is already rattled, with the VIX at 21.93 and up 27.43% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). A shutdown would also disrupt official data, which investors already worry about after the administration disbanded two expert panels on economic data [243].

Catalyst & Thesis: Dell raised its dividend 18% and launched a $10 billion buyback [120], after its full-year EPS beat expectations [119]. The thesis is that a company which beats and returns cash gets a bid under the shares while the orders keep coming.

Price Hurdle & Risk: Dell closed at 97.25 USD, down 15.91% over five sessions and down 4.35% over 20 sessions from 101.67 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The risk is the hardware sell-off that hit the AI complex the same week, when Nvidia fell 9% on tariff fears [123].

Trade Expression: Buy in two tranches on the five-session drawdown, and make the second tranche conditional on the next session holding the rebound. Invalidation is a further leg down that takes the shares below the five-session low, which would say the buyback is not enough.

Catalyst & Thesis: Wells Fargo kept its Buy rating on Eli Lilly and raised its target to $1,100 [167], while Novo Nordisk cut Wegovy prices after a similar move by Lilly [163] and offers cash-pay Wegovy at $499 a month [162]. The thesis is that Lilly’s volume gain outweighs the price cut.

Price Hurdle & Risk: Lilly closed at 929.72 USD, up 2.05% in the prior session and up 12.55% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The risk is that competition resets the pricing the multiple depends on.

Trade Expression: Own the shares on a pullback, and treat the 20-session reference of 826.07 USD as the invalidation: a close below it would undo the 20-session gain (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-04).

Catalyst & Thesis: Nvidia’s sales grew 78% with strong guidance [199], yet Reuters reported its optimistic forecast did not convince Wall Street [121], and Summit Insights downgraded the stock over AI market concerns [122]. The short thesis is that the stock has not repriced the downgrade.

Price Hurdle & Risk: Nvidia closed at 117.30 USD, up 1.13% in the prior session but down 10.65% over five sessions and down 1.14% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The risk is a squeeze back toward the 20-session reference of 118.65 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-04).

The thesis is the split: US capacity grows while the leading edge stays at home.

Price Hurdle & Risk: TSM closed at 184.28 USD, down 5.31% over five sessions and down 9.69% over 20 sessions from 204.05 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). TSMC’s shares slid to a four-month low even as Trump reportedly planned to announce a $100 billion US chip deal [245], which says the market has partly priced the split.

Trade Expression: Own the ADR on a close above the five-session low with a stop under it, and keep the position small while the split is unresolved. Invalidation is any statement that the leading edge is moving to the US.

Catalyst & Thesis: Analysts highlighted Credo’s hyperscaler partnerships with Amazon, Microsoft and xAI [246]. The thesis is that these partnerships give the revenue visibility the stock has not been paid for.

Price Hurdle & Risk: Credo closed at 46.73 USD, down 13.97% in the prior session, down 23.76% over five sessions and down 38.71% over 20 sessions from 76.25 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The risk is that the partnerships are already in the price and the drawdown has more to run.
Trade Expression: A small position only, and only after a session that closes off its low. Invalidation is another session as bad as the prior one, when the stock fell 13.97%.

Catalyst & Thesis: Wall Street’s top analysts upgraded Oracle, in a roundup of the day’s calls that also downgraded Dollar General [247]. The thesis is that the upgrade reprices the AI cloud business, which the stock has not been credited for.

Price Hurdle & Risk: Oracle closed at 161.56 USD, up 2.60% in the prior session and down 6.33% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The hurdle is the 20-session reference of 167.89 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-02-04).
Trade Expression: Buy on a close above the five-session high, with the 167.89 reference as the first target and the five-session low as the stop.

The dominant popular-narrative trade is China's AI push, in which the crowd buys Alibaba on its spending plan and its options chatter, the same mechanics as the DeepSeek debut, Nvidia's 2023 run and the 1999 internet-infrastructure trade: one story about who builds the next model, and a crowd that reads every new spending figure as the next leg.

Why Retail Is Here: The story retail tells itself is that China is back in the AI race, and Alibaba is the listed way to own it. Alibaba will spend more than $52 billion on AI and cloud over the next three years [248], and its shares soared nearly 15% after stellar earnings [249]. The crowd's anchor is the 20-session reference of 102.35 USD from 4 February, which the stock now sits far above (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Retail reads that distance as proof that the AI trade is not only an American one.

What Is Driving It: The hard evidence is in the price. Alibaba closed at 141.03 USD, up 8.61% in the prior session, up 1.40% over five sessions and up 37.79% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The catalyst in the headlines is the AI push: TradingView's market report said Alibaba jumps on AI push [55], and the spending behind it is the $52 billion AI and cloud plan [248]. The earnings base is older and mixed. Reuters reported that Alibaba shares opened at a three-year high as quarterly revenue rebounded [250], while Yahoo Finance's headline on the third quarter says earnings missed estimates even as revenues improved [251]. The move is not confined to one line. The Hang Seng is up 14.55% over 20 sessions and KWEB, the China internet ETF, is up 14.95%, while the Nasdaq 100 is down 4.35% over the same 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

The Social Signal: Attention shows up in the options tape. Moomoo's options chatter put Alibaba among the most active options after China's tech pledge, alongside Nvidia and Tesla [252], which puts the name in the same options conversation as Nvidia and Tesla. The consumer side is the same story. Yahoo Finance wrote that Tencent's AI bot passes DeepSeek as China's favourite on iPhones [253], and NPR's headline says Alibaba founder Jack Ma returns, five years after he largely disappeared from public view [254]. A founder coming back is the kind of headline retail repeats, because it gives the story a face.

Historical Analog: The closest mechanical analog is the DeepSeek debut, which the February coverage keeps returning to. The Guardian described Nvidia's first earnings after DeepSeek's AI debut [255], and Reuters framed Nvidia's earnings as a test of AI chip demand as DeepSeek sows spending doubts [256]. What happened first is that a Chinese model put doubt on the AI spending that US names were priced on. What came second is the search for the other side of that bet: Chinese AI platforms that the crowd reads as another way into the build-out. Alibaba is in that second wave for the same reason Tencent's bot is the favourite, because the story has moved from the model to the platform that serves it.

Smart Money View: The split is about pace, not direction. The bull case is the company's own plan, more than $52 billion over three years on AI and cloud [248], and a TradingView piece that calls the earnings surge strong growth with AI potential and undervalued upside [257]. The bear case is an analyst who says there is 'no clarity whatsoever' about Alibaba's future [258], and a third-quarter print that missed estimates [251]. Both sides accept that the spending is happening. They disagree on how fast it turns into earnings, which makes the institutional debate a question of timing rather than of whether the build-out is real.

When the Narrative Breaks: The line is the 20-session reference of 102.35 USD from 4 February, and a close back below it would erase the whole 37.79% gain (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The instrument risk is the listing. The Hong Kong line of the same company closed at 129.90 HKD, up 1.64% in the prior session but down 5.11% over five sessions, while the US line rose 1.40% over the same five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). A split like that is a sign the move is carried by trading interest as much as by the business. The dated test is in the product news: Tom's Hardware reported that Alibaba's RISC-V server CPU ships this month, with more designs to follow [259], so March shipments are the first check on whether the AI story has a product behind it. If the most-active list drops Alibaba, the attention will leave before the price does.

Why Retail Is Here: Palantir is the stock whose fans left after a plunge and were pulled back by a government story. Yahoo Finance wrote on 28 February that the plunge sent its biggest fans to the exits [260]. Then came DOGE: Investopedia's headline is that Palantir's stock surges as a Wall Street analyst says it could help DOGE cut spending [261], and Quartz reported that the stock pops 5% on an analyst's view that Pentagon cuts will not hurt it [262]. The crowd's anchor is the 103.83 USD reference from 4 February (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Where It Breaks: Palantir closed at 90.13 USD, up 6.79% in the prior session, up 0.92% over five sessions and down 13.19% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). A reclaim of 103.83 would say the fans are back, and a close back below the pre-pop level would hand back the 6.79% gain. The business test is in the headlines: Bloomberg's headline says Palantir will expand AI across financial firms through the TWG venture [263]. The instrument risk is that the crowd is split. Stocktwits carried a trading page for the Direxion Daily PLTR Bear 1X Shares fund [264], and a Yahoo Finance item said institutional investors in Palantir saw a US$40b decrease in market cap in the week before 27 February [265].

Why Retail Is Here: Retail's version of the reserve is that the state is about to buy. Fortune reported that bitcoin popped 6% after a top Trump official hinted the administration is about to reveal its crypto reserve strategy [214]. What changed since the early-March naming is the timing: Fortune's hint of a reveal and TradingView's report that the US is seen delaying it [216] both landed on 5 March. Robinhood is running a contest with $2 million in bitcoin prizes [266], and Michael Saylor says bitcoin is the only neutral asset for the US crypto reserve [267]. The crowd's anchor is the 96,623.87 close from 13 February (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Where It Breaks: Bitcoin closed at 90,623.56 USD, up 3.90% in the prior session and up 7.41% over five sessions, but down 6.21% over 20 sessions from the 96,623.87 reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Reclaiming that reference would mean the reserve premium is back. The downside trigger is the $78K retest that a TradingView trader is eyeing while the US is seen delaying the reserve [216]. The instrument risk is the proxy: IBIT, the iShares bitcoin trust, closed at 51.44 USD and is down 8.36% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

Why Retail Is Here: The Tesla slide is still the crowd's favourite dip, but India gives it a changed catalyst. Reuters reported that the US is weighing a zero tariff on cars in an India trade deal as Tesla's entry nears [268], and CNBC TV18 reported that UBS upgrades say the Tesla entry is not a threat [269]. The New York Times headlined buyer's remorse sinking in for Elon Musk's critics who own EVs [270], which keeps the brand story in the feed.

Where It Breaks: Tesla closed at 279.10 USD, up 2.60% in the prior session, down 4.02% over five sessions and down 28.84% over 20 sessions from 392.21 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The trigger is the 392.21 reference, which any rebound has to reclaim, and a close back below 279.10 would say the bounce has failed. The dated test is India, which the headlines describe as nearing rather than dated [268]. The sales base is the weak spot: Reuters reported that China-made EV sales fell to their lowest since August 2022 [158].

The iShares STOXX Europe 600 Automobiles & Parts ETF closed at 52.16 EUR, down 6.02% over five sessions and up 1.14% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Reuters reported that European auto stocks sank as US tariffs on Mexico and Canada kicked in [[n3261]].
Reported
Continental’s shares plunged on a revenue fall and soft guidance [[n2818]]. Mercedes is cutting headcount and lowering pay increases in its cost-cutting drive [[n2844]].
EPS Upside Watch

Volkswagen’s budget EV is the upside story. VW unveiled an entry-level EV aimed at squeezed European consumers [[n8689]], with a production version set to launch at around 20,000 euros [[n8708]]. Volkswagen closed at 105.55 EUR, up 13.03% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
⚡ Breaking Convention

The emissions rule is contested. One report says the Commission will water down auto emission targets [[n7728]], while another says the EU sticks to its zero-emission path for new cars [[n8378]]. The two readings do not settle the direction, so the sector’s multiple depends on which one the market believes.
Narrative

Semiconductors are caught between the AI cycle and the tariff map. The semiconductor ETF closed at 206.63 USD, down 5.19% over five sessions and 4.51% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). TSMC’s $100 billion US commitment is real, but it will not include the most advanced chips, Taiwan confirmed [[n4422]], and Qualcomm’s CEO welcomed the investment [[n7617]].
Reported
ASML’s annual report says export curbs hit customer spending in 2024 [[n8246]]. Nvidia and Broadcom are testing chips on Intel’s manufacturing process, sources said [[n2744]].
EPS Upside Watch

Nvidia’s China business is the upside watch, if the indirect channel holds. Tom’s Hardware reported that Chinese firms get Blackwell chips by ordering through nearby countries, defying US bans [[n1139]]. That is volume a tighter export rule would remove.
⚡ Breaking Convention

A Chinese scientist urged China to build an alternative to Nvidia’s CUDA software [[n8638]], which cuts against the software moat that supports the chip multiple. Investors cannot treat that moat as safe while an alternative is being pushed.

earnings_pattern.title: What the market pays for: forward numbers and cash return, not the beat
parts: Rewarded

Forward numbers and cash returns were rewarded. Rolls-Royce upgraded its forecasts and its shares soared over 18% [[n5745]]. Synopsys’s revenue forecast beat estimates on the AI chip boom, and the shares rose [[n2459]]. Snowflake posted a big earnings beat and the stock jumped [[n2445]]. Thales soared as its 2024 earnings beat forecasts on defence spending [[n2877]]. Dell lifted its dividend 18% and launched a $10 billion buyback [[n3567]] after its full-year EPS beat [[n0396]].
Punished

Beats with soft forward numbers were punished. Nvidia’s sales grew 78% with strong guidance [[n2423]], yet Reuters reported its optimistic forecast did not convince Wall Street [[n0390]], and the stock sank over 8% as earnings were no match for sky-high expectations [[n6326]]. Salesforce missed on revenue and issued disappointing guidance [[n2440]]. Norwegian Cruise Line’s shares fell despite an earnings beat [[n2622]].
Pattern

The pattern is that the market pays for the next quarter, not the last one. Trailing beats were ignored when the forward number was soft, and the rewards went to companies that raised forward numbers or returned cash. The sharpest disappointment came where the beat was already in the price. Nvidia dropped in the session after its optimistic report [[n0392]].
Attention into EPS

Attention is moving to the next print. Stocktwits flagged Vistra’s retail sentiment as bearish before its results, in the “mega growth” debate after DeepSeek [[n5764]]. Nvidia was downgraded by Summit Insights over AI market concerns [[n2743]]. The template for the next cycle is consumer guidance on tariffs: Best Buy’s warning that price increases were “highly likely” [[n2810]] is what investors will check first.
Playbook

Own the names that raise forward numbers or return cash, and sell the beats that come with soft guidance. Hedge the AI leaders into the next print, because a priced-in beat can cost 8% in a day, as Nvidia’s drop showed [[n6326]]. Trade the consumer names on tariff guidance rather than on the revenue line.

crypto.title: Bitcoin is a policy trade again, and the dip-buyers are being whipsawed
parts: Market Context

Bitcoin closed at 90,623.56 USD, up 3.90% in the latest session and 7.41% over five sessions, but down 6.21% over 20 sessions from 96,623.87 on February 13 (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-05). Hold bitcoin in spot-type vehicles, size for a retest of $78K, and add only when ETF inflows return and open interest rebuilds. Treat Strategy as a levered proxy: its 20-session decline of 11.42% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05) is what leverage looks like on the way down. Trim into the reserve pops. The 96,623.87 February reference is the line: above it the reserve premium is back, below it the trade is a fade.

flows.title: Liquidity is abundant, the dollar is the swing, and buybacks are the bid
parts: Global Liquidity

Liquidity is still abundant even as policy tightens at the margin. The New York Fed’s Perli said market liquidity levels remain abundant [[n3785]]. India’s central bank announced an infusion of over $21 billion to support growth [[n3773]] and signalled it wants a banking-system liquidity surplus [[n3774]]. The Boston Fed’s work on dealer risk constraints shows that relaxing them can make the Treasury market more liquid [[n3677]], which matters because a crowded trade depends on that plumbing. The euro area is on the same plumbing, with the ECB publishing its January bank rate statistics [[n1443]].
Rates & Dollar

The dollar is the swing factor. The dollar index is at 105.74 index points, down 2.06% over 20 sessions and down 0.64% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). CoinDesk reported the index declining below 105 as bitcoin surged past $88,000 [[n10389]], and a Reuters poll says the dollar will lose its lustre on trade war jitters [[n3812]]. Long bonds are the other side of the trade: TLT closed at 90.70 USD, up 2.57% over 20 sessions, and IEF at 94.56 USD, up 1.66% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). On the curve, the two-year is down 22 bps and the 10-year down 24 bps over 20 observations, a bull flattening (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05). Reuters reported that parts of the Treasury market are concerned about a pause in rate cuts [[n10321]].
Credit Check

Credit is wider in the middle of the market. Bloomberg reported that credit spreads are on their longest widening streak since 2023 [[n3564]], and Fitch says credit card performance is deteriorating [[n1439]]. High yield has held: HYG closed at 79.62 USD, up 0.14% over 20 sessions and down 0.55% over five, while investment-grade LQD closed at 108.83 USD, up 1.28% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The junk market has not yet followed the widening. In Europe, Italy’s spread over Germany has dropped below 100 basis points [[n3324]], so the regional credit picture is not uniform.
Equity & Fund Flows

Buybacks are the main equity bid. Dell raised its dividend 18% and launched a $10 billion buyback [[n3567]], and Trip.com announced a US$400M buyback as its stock fell 12% [[n3637]]. AppLovin’s shares bounced back after its buyback news [[n3545]], and LSEG’s shares rose on a $633.8 million buyback [[n2519]]. Fund flows are mixed: spot bitcoin ETFs have seen record outflows [[n1548]], and inflows returned once an 8-day outflow streak ended [[n1637]]. The strategists are cautious. MarketWatch wrote that Wall Street’s biggest bear says the S&P 500 could drop to 4,200 [[n3815]], and Goldman Sachs warned the rally may falter after a 5% selloff [[n10217]]. The S&P 500 is down 3.23% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Hedge funds had a rough February as well, with the sector’s biggest names stung in the month [[n3585]].
Portfolio Implication

Keep equity at market weight, hedge tail risk, and prefer buyback-backed earnings over momentum with no cash behind it. Own duration: a bull flattening with the long end leading is money moving into the long end, and the 10-year is down 24 bps over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-05). Keep credit beta small until spreads stop widening. The conditional is the dollar: a break below 105 would help emerging-market hard-currency debt, where EMB closed at 91.28 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Cash is a position too: Berkshire Hathaway’s market value reached $1.07 trillion, surpassing Tesla [[n2692]], and Barron’s noted that Warren Buffett has been selling stocks [[n10405]].

anticipatory.title: The next US jobs report
parts: What Is Priced

The market is pricing a soft payroll print. Conditional Expression

If the next jobs report confirms the ADP slowdown, the front end rallies and the flattening deepens, so buy duration on the weak print and avoid steepeners. If hiring holds, the two-year should retrace part of its 22 bps fall, and the dollar index at 105.74 index points would firm again (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
Risk

anticipatory.title: The tariff clock

The risk is that a stock up 60.59% in 20 sessions has priced the package before it is law. Bloomberg reported that East German voters complicate Merz’s plan to boost Ukraine defence [[n3157]], which is the political drag.

anticipatory.title: The US funding fight

Shutdown risk is back on the table. Axios reported that Republicans are hunting for Democratic votes to avoid one [[n10295]].
Conditional Expression

If Republicans find the votes, the shutdown premium fades and the safe-haven bid in gold and Treasuries comes off. If they do not, expect the bid to return, with gold at 2,926.00 USD as the cleanest hedge (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).

The risk is a political shock landing on a tape that is already rattled, with the VIX at 21.93 and up 27.43% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). A shutdown would also disrupt official data, which investors already worry about after the administration disbanded two expert panels on economic data [[n10352]].

catalysts.title: $DELL — the buyback is the thesis

spec.retail_intro: The dominant popular-narrative trade is China's AI push, in which the crowd buys Alibaba on its spending plan and its options chatter, the same mechanics as the DeepSeek debut, Nvidia's 2023 run and the 1999 internet-infrastructure trade: one story about who builds the next model, and a crowd that reads every new spending figure as the next leg.

retail.title: Alibaba / BABA — China's AI push is back
parts: Why Retail Is Here

The story retail tells itself is that China is back in the AI race, and Alibaba is the listed way to own it. Alibaba will spend more than $52 billion on AI and cloud over the next three years [[n2178]], and its shares soared nearly 15% after stellar earnings [[n1997]]. The crowd's anchor is the 20-session reference of 102.35 USD from 4 February, which the stock now sits far above (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). Retail reads that distance as proof that the AI trade is not only an American one.
What Is Driving It

The hard evidence is in the price. Alibaba closed at 141.03 USD, up 8.61% in the prior session, up 1.40% over five sessions and up 37.79% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The catalyst in the headlines is the AI push: TradingView's market report said Alibaba jumps on AI push [[n1382]], and the spending behind it is the $52 billion AI and cloud plan [[n2178]]. The earnings base is older and mixed. Reuters reported that Alibaba shares opened at a three-year high as quarterly revenue rebounded [[n1995]], while Yahoo Finance's headline on the third quarter says earnings missed estimates even as revenues improved [[n2079]]. The move is not confined to one line. The Hang Seng is up 14.55% over 20 sessions and KWEB, the China internet ETF, is up 14.95%, while the Nasdaq 100 is down 4.35% over the same 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
The Social Signal

Attention shows up in the options tape. Moomoo's options chatter put Alibaba among the most active options after China's tech pledge, alongside Nvidia and Tesla [[n1377]], which puts the name in the same options conversation as Nvidia and Tesla. The consumer side is the same story. Yahoo Finance wrote that Tencent's AI bot passes DeepSeek as China's favourite on iPhones [[n1186]], and NPR's headline says Alibaba founder Jack Ma returns, five years after he largely disappeared from public view [[n1042]]. A founder coming back is the kind of headline retail repeats, because it gives the story a face.
Historical Analog

The closest mechanical analog is the DeepSeek debut, which the February coverage keeps returning to. The Guardian described Nvidia's first earnings after DeepSeek's AI debut [[n2420]], and Reuters framed Nvidia's earnings as a test of AI chip demand as DeepSeek sows spending doubts [[n2230]]. What happened first is that a Chinese model put doubt on the AI spending that US names were priced on. What came second is the search for the other side of that bet: Chinese AI platforms that the crowd reads as another way into the build-out. Alibaba is in that second wave for the same reason Tencent's bot is the favourite, because the story has moved from the model to the platform that serves it.
Smart Money View

The split is about pace, not direction. The bull case is the company's own plan, more than $52 billion over three years on AI and cloud [[n2178]], and a TradingView piece that calls the earnings surge strong growth with AI potential and undervalued upside [[n1073]]. The bear case is an analyst who says there is 'no clarity whatsoever' about Alibaba's future [[n1043]], and a third-quarter print that missed estimates [[n2079]]. Both sides accept that the spending is happening. They disagree on how fast it turns into earnings, which makes the institutional debate a question of timing rather than of whether the build-out is real.
When the Narrative Breaks

The line is the 20-session reference of 102.35 USD from 4 February, and a close back below it would erase the whole 37.79% gain (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). The instrument risk is the listing. The Hong Kong line of the same company closed at 129.90 HKD, up 1.64% in the prior session but down 5.11% over five sessions, while the US line rose 1.40% over the same five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). A split like that is a sign the move is carried by trading interest as much as by the business. The dated test is in the product news: Tom's Hardware reported that Alibaba's RISC-V server CPU ships this month, with more designs to follow [[n1107]], so March shipments are the first check on whether the AI story has a product behind it. If the most-active list drops Alibaba, the attention will leave before the price does.

retail.title: Palantir / PLTR — the fans came back on DOGE talk
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Palantir is the stock whose fans left after a plunge and were pulled back by a government story. Yahoo Finance wrote on 28 February that the plunge sent its biggest fans to the exits [[n5795]]. Then came DOGE: Investopedia's headline is that Palantir's stock surges as a Wall Street analyst says it could help DOGE cut spending [[n6108]], and Quartz reported that the stock pops 5% on an analyst's view that Pentagon cuts will not hurt it [[n2747]]. The crowd's anchor is the 103.83 USD reference from 4 February (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
Where It Breaks

Palantir closed at 90.13 USD, up 6.79% in the prior session, up 0.92% over five sessions and down 13.19% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05). A reclaim of 103.83 would say the fans are back, and a close back below the pre-pop level would hand back the 6.79% gain. The business test is in the headlines: Bloomberg's headline says Palantir will expand AI across financial firms through the TWG venture [[n6107]]. The instrument risk is that the crowd is split. Stocktwits carried a trading page for the Direxion Daily PLTR Bear 1X Shares fund [[n6055]], and a Yahoo Finance item said institutional investors in Palantir saw a US$40b decrease in market cap in the week before 27 February [[n10033]].

retail.title: Bitcoin / BTC — the reserve reveal is still coming
parts: Why Retail Is Here

Retail's version of the reserve is that the state is about to buy. Fortune reported that bitcoin popped 6% after a top Trump official hinted the administration is about to reveal its crypto reserve strategy [[n1909]]. What changed since the early-March naming is the timing: Fortune's hint of a reveal and TradingView's report that the US is seen delaying it [[n1910]] both landed on 5 March. Robinhood is running a contest with $2 million in bitcoin prizes [[n6112]], and Michael Saylor says bitcoin is the only neutral asset for the US crypto reserve [[n1949]]. The crowd's anchor is the 96,623.87 close from 13 February (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-05).
Where It Breaks
